title: Justice Department Lets Stand Ruling That H-1B-Only Job Ads Are Not Illegal Alone
excerpt: An administrative ruling dismissing a complaint over a Chicago H-1B jobs board survives after Attorney General Todd Blanche declined review, narrowing how targeted ads can be challenged.
body:
• Attorney General Todd Blanche let the 60-day review window lapse on an August 12 administrative law judge ruling, leaving it in force, according to IANS.
  • The ruling dismissed US Tech Workers' complaint over Boston Consulting Group's role in the P33 Chicago H-1B Connect jobs board, holding discriminatory advertising is not a standalone cause of action under the Immigration and Nationality Act.
  • Thirteen House Republicans, led by Paul Gosar and Chip Roy, had asked the Justice Department on October 9 to take up the case.
  • For Indian professionals — over 70 per cent of H-1B holders — ads targeting visa holders alone are now harder to challenge; a US worker must tie the ad to an actual nonselection, recruitment or termination claim.

The US Justice Department has allowed a ruling to stand that job advertisements aimed only at H-1B visa holders do not, by themselves, amount to illegal discrimination against American workers, IANS reported on October 21. Attorney General Todd Blanche let lapse the 60-day window to review an August 12 decision by an administrative law judge in the department's Office of the Chief Administrative Hearing Officer (OCAHO), despite a request from 13 House Republicans to take up the case, according to Breitbart News coverage cited by IANS.

What the judge decided

The judge dismissed a complaint by US Tech Workers against Boston Consulting Group over its participation in "P33 Chicago H-1B Connect," a Chicago initiative that served as a jobs board for H-1B visa holders. The ruling held that "discriminatory advertising does not represent a discrete cause of action under the INA." Such evidence, it said, is limited to part of a case alleging nonselection, recruitment or termination, rather than an independently actionable violation.

"The Department thoroughly reviewed the ALJ's decision and stakeholder concerns, and ultimately determined that the underlying decision was consistent with OCAHO precedent."

— US Department of Justice, via Breitbart News

The department added that it "aggressively targets employers who discriminate against American workers through unlawful hiring practices."

The pushback

In their October 9 letter to Blanche, the lawmakers led by Representatives Paul Gosar and Chip Roy said the decision "suggests that section 274B does not provide a cause of action for discriminatory advertising." "If employers can expressly target foreign workers while discouraging Americans from applying, those protections are substantially weakened," they wrote. John Miano, a lawyer for US Tech Workers, told Breitbart News that "the whole 25 years of prosecuting companies" over such practices "is set back 25 years by this."

Enforcement has not stopped elsewhere

Hi India reported the ruling came the same day the department announced online grocery company Instacart would pay $5 million to settle charges that it discriminated against American workers while recruiting for green-card-linked jobs under the PERM programme. Last week, data company Cloudera agreed to a two-year bar from the PERM programme in a similar case.

The distinction matters for the diaspora. Indians make up the largest share of H-1B visa holders, accounting for more than 70 per cent of approved petitions in recent years, and most employment-based green card applicants from India move through the PERM route. The ruling raises the legal bar for challenging H-1B-focused job boards such as the Chicago initiative: a US worker must now show actual harm in hiring or recruitment, not just a targeted advertisement. Employers, meanwhile, still face PERM and hiring-practice enforcement of the kind that produced the Instacart and Cloudera outcomes — the ad alone is no longer the case, but the hiring decision still can be.
